rows.evidence: Q1: Annex 1 (Tables A1-A4, Figs A3-A7) reports the authors' own field discharge records at the head of district 4 of the Sinistra Ofanto scheme (1991) used to calibrate the Clement model; Chapter 4 (Fig. 45) reports the authors' own sensitivity runs of ELIDM with 50 sets of random flow regimes; Chapter 5 reports applications of COPAM/AKLA to the Lecce network and a 582 ha network.
rows.notes: The document is an FAO/CIHEAM technical paper (I&D Paper 59) that is largely a methodology and software (COPAM) manual, so Q1 is borderline; it was rated 'yes' because it embeds original model runs and field data (Annex 1 calibration, Fig. 34, Fig. 45 cost analyses, Figs 69-77). On the claim itself, the study does not compare the investment cost of on-demand networks with that of rotation or other delivery-schedule networks, nor does it report that on-demand networks cost more. It computes network costs for on-demand designs (e.g. 126 million ITL in Box 3, 207 million ITL in Annex 3) and shows (Fig. 45) that optimal network cost rises and stabilises as more flow regimes are required to be satisfied, and it notes (Chapter 3, drawing on FAO Paper 44) that the elasticity eR measures the over-capacity characteristic of on-demand operation; but these are design results for on-demand networks, not an own finding that their investment cost is 'usually higher' than alternatives. Chapter 6 remarks that extending the pipe network to every small farm is expensive, but this is a general statement from FAO (1990), not an own result. Hence Q2 'no'.

notes: Full text appears complete (front matter, six chapters, bibliography and three annexes); figures are described only by captions. The study is a hybrid guideline/manual with embedded original analyses on hydraulic performance and pipe-size optimisation of on-demand pressurised networks; it contains no comparative investment-cost analysis of on-demand versus other delivery schedules.
